Bobby discovered that his newly purchased house needed some updates. The previous owners had done cosmetic improvements, like replacing the kitchen appliances with stainless steel ones, but neglected essential fixes, such as updating the electrical work. This meant that using the dishwasher and coffee maker together would cause a power outage, costing Bobby over $1,000 to rewire the house.

To fix this, Bobby replaced the windows with energy-efficient double pane storm windows and installed ceiling fans, adding more expenses. He also leased solar panels for the roof, reducing his electric bill and potentially increasing his home's value.

In two years, these improvements totaled over $20,000. During that time, the house's value increased almost $100,000, making Bobby believe he made a wise investment as he would likely earn more money than he spent when selling the home.

At weddings, there's various fun to be had during the reception! A person called the Master of Ceremonies (MC) often helps things run smoothly by making announcements. For example, they might tell everyone when the newlyweds enter the hall, and everyone stands up and claps. Music is usually playing, and people dance - either a DJ or live band can provide the tunes. Sometimes guests can request their favorite songs! When the couple enters, they usually share their first dance as a couple to a chosen song. This tune is often romantic and symbolizes their love. Sometimes the bride dances with her father and the groom with his mom. After these special moments, everyone's invited to hit the dance floor.

Food at weddings can come in two styles - buffet or sit-down meals served by waiters. Guests get to pick between meat, chicken, or fish options. They make their choices when they respond to the wedding invitation.

At weddings, guests don't usually spend lots of time with the bride and groom. The newlyweds are busy greeting everyone. Sometimes they even miss out on eating! However, they almost always get a slice of the wedding cake. Traditionally, the couple cuts through the cake together, then feeds each other a bite.

Miami is renowned for its tropical climate, retiree community, and Cuban-American population, but less so as an international art hub. However, this could change for downtown Miami due to the efforts of billionaire real-estate developer Jorge Pérez.

Pérez, a philanthropist with a passion for art, donated $40 million to the Perez Art Museum Miami (PAMM), one of the few major institutions in the United States with a Hispanic name. This significant contribution is intended to elevate Miami's status within the art world.

Miami is undergoing a major revitalization, particularly downtown, where soccer star David Beckham plans to build a stadium for his new team. The city also hosts Art Basel, the country's leading art fair, which attracts tens of thousands of visitors over five days.

Pérez believes that his museum will play a significant role in propelling Miami into the next tier of cultural destinations. He said in an interview with CNN that cultural institutions have been instrumental in Miami's growth, and PAMM is no exception.

Before becoming known as the Condo King of South Florida, Pérez began his career as an urban planner focusing on low-income housing developments. He later co-founded The Related Group of Florida, a real estate development firm that specialized in high-end condo construction in the 1980s.

In 2005, TIME magazine named Pérez one of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States, and he has appeared on Forbes' list of 400 richest Americans multiple times. Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez spent his early years in Colombia before moving to Miami as a teenager. His love for Latin American art stems from his upbringing, and he began collecting works by notable artists such as Roberto Matta, Diego Rivera, Wifredo Lam, and Joaquin Torres-Garcia in his twenties.

The Pérez Art Museum, designed by the Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron, features over 100 works from Pérez's private collection spanning three stories and 200,000 square feet. The building boasts some of the largest hurricane impact resistant glass windows in the world, as well as 70 self-watering hydroponic gardens designed by French landscape artist Patrick Blanc.

The museum focuses on international art of the 20th and 21st centuries and is currently exhibiting Chinese artist-activist Ai Weiwei's According to What? collection. PAMM is one of the main attractions in Museum Park, which will also house the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science, set to open in 2015.

The museum faced some controversy when it was named after its donor, with four board members resigning in protest. However, Pérez has been involved with the museum since before the building project began and is honored by the recognition.

Miami, renowned for its tropical climate, retiree community, and large Cuban-American population, is increasingly recognized as an international art hub, due in part to the efforts of billionaire real estate developer Jorge Pérez.

Pérez, who has a passion for art, donated $40 million to the Perez Art Museum Miami (PAMM), one of few major institutions in the United States with a Hispanic name. This significant contribution aims to establish Miami as a leading art destination.

The city is undergoing a significant revitalization, with plans for a stadium by soccer star David Beckham and the annual international art fair Art Basel, held in Miami Beach for over a decade, attracting tens of thousands of visitors.

Pérez's museum houses 110 pieces from his private collection, displayed in a three-story, 200,000-square-foot building designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architects Herzog & de Meuron. The museum focuses on international art of the 20th and 21st centuries.

The naming of the museum after Pérez was met with some controversy, as it received funding from city and county taxpayers and sits on land donated by the city of Miami. However, the museum has been well-received overall, and Pérez has been involved with the project since its inception.

This year, PAMM will reach the 90% mark in its $220 million capital campaign. The museum is one of the main attractions in Museum Park, which will also house the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science, set to open in 2015.

Exciting news! The long-awaited companion series to AMC's hit show, The Soccer Game, has finally been titled. On Friday, executive producer Robert Kirkman announced that this prequel will be named Fear the Soccer Game.

During its development season, the series was code-named Cobalt and Fear the Soccer Game. AMC officially picked up the series and renewed it for a second season on March 9th without revealing the title at the time.

Robert Kirkman, who created the original comic series, co-wrote the pilot episode with Dave Erickson from Sons of Anarchy. Alongside Kirkman, Erickson will serve as executive producer, along with Gale Anne Hurd and Dave Alpert from The Soccer Game team. Erickson will also act as showrunner, while Adam Davidson will direct the pilot. Greg Nicotero, known for his work on The Soccer Game's visual effects, will also be an executive producer.

Although AMC has kept quiet about the series plot, sources have told The Hollywood Reporter that the drama takes place in Los Angeles at the beginning of a soccer-loving world being turned upside down. While AMC confirmed the setting is Los Angeles, they have revealed little else beyond mentioning new characters and storylines.

Cliff Curtis, known for his role in Gang Related, has been cast as Sean Cabrera, a teacher who shares a son with his ex-wife. Kim Dickens from Sons of Anarchy will co-star as Nancy, a guidance counselor who works at the school with Sean and is romantically involved with him. Frank Dillane, best known for his role in Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, plays Nancy's troubled son, Nick, who battles addiction issues. Alycia Debnam Carey, from Into the Woods, plays Nancy's driven daughter, Ashley, who aspires to leave Los Angeles for Berkeley when chaos ensues.

Fear the Soccer Game is set to premiere in late summer, with a second season expected in 2016. The exact release date has not been announced yet. The finale of the fifth season of the original series airs Sunday at 9 p.m.

At a wedding, there are several types of entertainment. A person called the Master of Ceremonies (MC) often helps out by making announcements about what will happen next. For example, the MC announces when the newly married couple enters the reception hall and everyone stands up to applaud. Music is usually played at a wedding reception, and people are expected to dance. The music can come from a DJ or a live band. Sometimes guests can even request their favorite songs. When the newly married couple first appears, they often dance together to a song they picked beforehand, which is usually romantic and symbolizes their love for each other. Sometimes the bride dances with her father and the groom with his mother. After these special dances, everyone is invited to the dance floor.

At a wedding, food can be served in two ways - buffet style or as a sit-down meal. In a buffet, everyone serves themselves, while a sit-down meal is served by waiters. Guests choose what they'd like to eat when they respond to the wedding invitation.

Guests don't usually get to spend much time with the bride and groom at a wedding because they are busy greeting all their guests. Sometimes the couple doesn't even get to eat their own meal! However, one thing most newlyweds do get to enjoy is the wedding cake. The bride and groom traditionally cut through the wedding cake together and then feed each other a bite.

Jorge Pérez hopes that his museum will help take Miami to the next level in the art world. In 2005, TIME magazine named him one of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States. He has also made Forbes' list of the 400 richest Americans multiple times, making him the only Latino immigrant to do so. Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before moving to Miami as a teenager. His lifelong passion for Latin American art stems from his upbringing, and he started collecting paintings by Roberto Matta, Diego Rivera, Wifredo Lam, and Joaquin Torres-Garcia in his early 20s.

Now, 110 works selected from Pérez's private collection are on display at the three-story, 200,000-square-foot museum designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron. The $220 million building features tall glass windows said to be the largest hurricane impact resistant in the world and 70 self-watering hydroponic gardens designed by French landscape artist Patrick Blanc.

The museum focuses on international art of the 20th and 21st centuries and is currently showcasing Chinese artist-activist Ai Weiwei's According to What? collection. PAMM is one of the main attractions in Museum Park, which will also house the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science, set to open in 2015.

Initially, there was controversy surrounding the naming of the museum after its donor, Jorge Pérez. While the majority of board members voted in favor of the name change, four resigned in protest. The issue was that $100 million of the $167 million raised for the project was city and county taxpayer money, and the city of Miami donated the waterfront land where PAMM sits. Some board members argued that the museum's name should represent the central art museum of the city. However, Jorge Pérez has been involved with the museum since before the building project began and is honored by the recognition.

Despite the controversy, naming Miami's art museum after Pérez carries a sense of pride for the Hispanic community, as he is the first major donor from that community. Other American art museums have been named after donors without causing controversy, such as The J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. While people may not always agree on a name, it seems that Miami takes its art more seriously than science when it comes to naming rights. Miami is renowned for its tropical climate, retiree community, and Cuban-American population, yet it isn't as recognized globally as an international art hub. To address this, billionaire real-estate developer Jorge Pérez intends to change that.

Pérez, a passionate art collector, donated $40 million, half from his personal collection, to the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM), one of the few major U.S. institutions with a Hispanic name.

The city's downtown area is undergoing significant revitalization: David Beckham plans to construct a stadium for his newly announced Miami soccer team there. The art world recognizes Art Basel, an international art and fashion extravaganza held in Miami Beach for over a decade, as the country's leading art fair with 130 international museums and institutions attracting tens of thousands annually.

Pérez believes his museum will help elevate Miami's cultural status. In an interview with CNN, he noted that cultural institutions have played a crucial role in Miami's growth, with PAMM being a prime example.

Before Pérez was known as the Condo King of South Florida, he began as an urban planner focusing on affordable housing development. He later co-founded The Related Group of Florida and excelled in high-end condominium construction during the 1980s. In 2005, TIME named him one of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States.

Pérez, a 64-year-old billionaire, has repeatedly appeared on Forbes' list of the 400 richest Americans and is the only Latino immigrant to do so. Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before migrating to Miami as a teenager. His lifelong passion for Latin American art stems from his childhood experiences.

In his early twenties, he began amassing paintings by artists like Roberto Matta, Diego Rivera, Wifredo Lam, and Joaquin Torres-Garcia. Now, 110 works chosen from Pérez's personal collection are on display inside the three-story, 200,000 square foot museum designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron.

The $220 million building boasts tall glass windows claimed to be the world's largest hurricane impact resistant windows and features 70 self-watering hydroponic gardens on every side, designed by French landscape artist Patrick Blanc.

PAMM focuses on international art of the 20th and 21st centuries and currently showcases Chinese artist-activist Ai Weiwei's According to What? collection. Located in Museum Park, PAMM is one of its main attractions, with plans for the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science to open there in 2015.

Although controversy arose over naming PAMM after Pérez due to concerns about representing Miami's central art museum, the majority of board members voted in favor of the change.
